subject: physics
question_text: Derive an expression for the pressure of an ideal gas on the basis of kinetic theory of gases. Hence give the kinetic interpretation of temperature.

verification.note: Sourced from the Sri Chaitanya IPE Study Material for Jr. Students 2026-27 edition, physics volume, Chapter 13 Long Answer Question 1 (printed p.141). Only the question was taken; the answer, its steps and its mark split are original work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. The eight 1-mark step split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. Physics hand-checked: the momentum change per collision (−2 m v_x), the hit frequency (v_x / 2L), the force from one molecule (m v_x² / L), the isotropy step (Σv_x² = ⅓Σv²), the boxed result P = ⅓(N/V)mv̄², the energy rewrite PV = ⅔N(½mv̄²), and the final comparison with PV = Nk_BT giving ½mv̄² = (3/2)k_BT all match the standard NCERT Class-11 Chapter 13 derivation.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.

steps.label: The model and its assumptions
lines: Consider N identical molecules, each
of mass m, contained in a cube of side L;
their size is negligible compared with
the distance between them, and they
move randomly. Every collision, wall or
molecule, is treated as perfectly elastic.
steps.margin_note: First mark. Name every assumption: point-sized molecules, random motion, and elastic collisions.
steps.why: The whole derivation rests on these three facts — a molecule carries no internal energy loss, so no kinetic energy is lost in a collision, and the wall receives back exactly what each molecule delivers.
common_mistakes: Leaving out that the collisions are elastic — an inelastic collision would lose kinetic energy at every bounce.

Thinking molecule-molecule collisions must be tracked separately — they are elastic between identical masses, so a collision only exchanges velocities and leaves the momentum delivered to the wall unchanged; the point-size assumption is about neglecting molecular volume beside the container volume.

recall.must_convey: That the model is N identical molecules of mass m in a cube of side L, point-sized, moving randomly, with every collision perfectly elastic.
accept: point-sized molecules moving randomly
every collision is perfectly elastic
N molecules of mass m in a cube of side L
first I state the model and its assumptions
molecules are treated as point particles
reject: pressure equals one third N over V m v bar squared
the wall receives twice m v x

steps.memory_tip: Three words to say: point-sized, random, elastic.

steps.label: Draw the figure
steps.margin_note: Not marked, but draw it — the wall and the two velocity arrows make every later step easier to follow.
steps.why: A molecule hitting a wall and rebounding is easier to reason about once it is drawn — the same picture is what the how-often and total-force steps refer back to for the wall and its area.
common_mistakes: Drawing the molecule hitting a corner or edge instead of the flat wall face — the derivation is about one wall, perpendicular to x.
Forgetting to show BOTH arrows — the incoming velocity and the rebound are two separate ideas worth remembering, even though this step itself carries no mark.

recall.must_convey: That a figure is drawn at this point, showing the cube, the wall, and the molecule's velocity before and after it hits the wall.
accept: then I draw the figure
draw the cube with the molecule and the wall
sketch the box and the incoming and rebound arrows
draw the wall and the velocity vectors
diagram of the molecule hitting the wall

force is m v x squared by L

steps.memory_tip: Draw the wall as a flat face of the cube, and the two arrows on the SAME line: one in, one back out.

steps.label: One collision
lines: Take one molecule with x-velocity v_x
hitting the wall perpendicular to x.
It rebounds elastically with velocity
−v_x, so its momentum change is
By Newton's third law, the wall gains
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Momentum reverses along x only; the wall receives what the molecule loses.
steps.why: The wall cannot simply absorb the hit — by Newton's third law it must receive exactly the momentum the molecule gave up, and that momentum is what becomes pressure.
common_mistakes: Writing the momentum change as −m v_x instead of −2 m v_x — the velocity reverses, so the change is twice v_x, not once.
Forgetting Newton's third law and stating the wall's momentum gain without justifying it.

recall.must_convey: That a molecule's x-momentum changes by −2 m v_x on rebound, and the wall gains +2 m v_x by Newton's third law.
accept: momentum change is minus two m v x
the molecule rebounds with minus v x
the wall gains two m v x by newton's third law
velocity reverses so the change is two m v x
delta p of the molecule is minus two m v x
reject: time between hits is two L by v x
force is m v x squared by L

steps.memory_tip: Velocity reverses, so momentum changes by 2 m v_x, not m v_x.

steps.label: How often
lines: Between two hits on this wall the
molecule crosses the cube and returns,
a distance 2L along x.
So the number of hits per second on
this wall is
steps.margin_note: Third mark. The round trip to the far wall and back is 2L, not L.
steps.why: The force on the wall depends on how OFTEN the molecule arrives, not just how hard — so the time between hits has to be worked out before the force can be.
common_mistakes: Using L instead of 2L — the molecule must reach the opposite wall and come back before it can hit this wall again.
Writing the frequency as 2L/v_x instead of its reciprocal v_x/2L.

recall.must_convey: That the round trip between hits on the same wall is 2L, giving v_x over 2L hits per second.
accept: the round trip is two L
time between hits is two L by v x
hits per second is v x by two L
the molecule crosses the cube and comes back
frequency is v x over two L
reject: force is m v x squared by L
delta p is two m v x

steps.memory_tip: The round trip is 2L, so hits per second is v_x over 2L — the reciprocal of the round-trip time.

steps.label: Force from one molecule
lines: Force is momentum delivered per
second: multiply the momentum per hit
by the number of hits per second.
steps.margin_note: Fourth mark. Force is the RATE of momentum delivery — momentum per hit times hits per second.
steps.why: Force is defined as the rate of change of momentum, so multiplying one hit's momentum by how often hits occur turns the single-collision result into a continuous force.
common_mistakes: Multiplying by the number of MOLECULES here — this step is still about the ONE molecule; the sum over N comes next.
Dropping the factor of 2 carried over from the momentum change in the previous step.

recall.must_convey: That the force from one molecule is momentum per hit times hits per second, giving F = m v_x squared over L.
accept: force equals momentum delivered per second
multiply two m v x by v x over two L
F equals m v x squared by L
force from one molecule is m v x squared over L
rate of momentum delivery gives the force
reject: hits per second is v x by two L
pressure is F over L squared
heard_as: m v x squared by L

steps.memory_tip: Force = momentum per hit × hits per second = 2mv_x × v_x/2L = m v_x²/L.

steps.label: Total force and pressure
lines: Summing this force over all N
molecules in the gas,
Pressure is force per unit area,
and this wall has area L²:

lines.text: P = F / L² = (m / L³) Σ v_x²

lines: Since the cube has volume V = L³,
steps.margin_note: Fifth mark. Write L³ as V explicitly — this is where the volume enters the formula.
steps.why: Adding up one molecule's force N times, then dividing by the wall's area, turns a single collision into the measurable pressure of the whole gas.
common_mistakes: Leaving the answer as F/L² without ever substituting L³ = V.
Dividing by the wrong area — the wall the molecule strikes has area L², not L³.

recall.must_convey: That summing the force over N molecules and dividing by wall area L squared gives P = (m/V) times sum of v_x squared, using V = L cubed.
accept: sum the force over N molecules
pressure is force over L squared
L cubed is the volume V
P equals m over V times sum v x squared
total force is m over L times sum v x squared

steps.memory_tip: Pressure is force over area L²; write L³ as V and the volume appears.

steps.label: Isotropy
lines: Motion is random, so no direction is
special: the three sums are equal,
The mean square speed is v̄² = Σv² / N,
so P = (m/V) Σ v_x² becomes
This may also be written P = ⅓ ρ v̄²,
where ρ = Nm/V is the gas density.
steps.margin_note: Sixth mark. This is the boxed formula; the density form P = ⅓ρv̄² is worth adding, but the mark is on P = ⅓(N/V)mv̄².
steps.why: Nothing in the physics singles out the x-direction — the molecule's speed is shared equally, on average, among the three directions it can move in, which is exactly why Σv_x² can be replaced by one third of Σv².
common_mistakes: Assuming Σv_x² = Σv_y² = Σv_z² without stating WHY — it follows from random motion, not from any calculation.
Writing ⅓Nv̄² instead of ⅓(N/V)mv̄² — the mass m and the volume V must both appear.

recall.must_convey: That random motion makes the three directional sums equal, giving the boxed result P = one third (N/V) m v bar squared.
accept: motion is random so the three sums are equal
each direction gets one third of sigma v squared
P equals one third N over V m v bar squared
pressure equals one third rho v bar squared
isotropy gives the factor of one third
reject: PV equals two thirds N times half m v bar squared
half m v bar squared equals three halves k B T
heard_as: P equals one third N over V m v bar squared

steps.memory_tip: Random motion shares Σv² equally three ways, so one wall's sum is one third of the total: P = ⅓(N/V)mv̄².

steps.label: Rewrite as energy
lines: Multiply the boxed result by V:
Write this as two-thirds of the
kinetic energy per molecule:
PV is two-thirds of the total
translational kinetic energy of the gas.
steps.margin_note: Seventh mark. This energy form is what gets compared with the ideal gas equation next.
steps.why: Multiplying by V turns the pressure formula into one written in the total kinetic energy of the gas, which is the form that compares directly with the ideal gas equation PV = Nk_BT.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to insert the ½ — the identity is ⅓mv̄² = ⅔(½mv̄²), not ⅔mv̄².
Calling ½mv̄² the energy of ALL the molecules — it is the average energy of ONE molecule.

recall.must_convey: That PV = one third N m v bar squared can be rewritten as two thirds N times half m v bar squared, the average kinetic energy per molecule.
accept: PV equals two thirds N half m v bar squared
multiply by V and rewrite with a half
pressure times volume is two thirds the kinetic energy
one third becomes two thirds of a half
PV in terms of average kinetic energy
reject: P equals one third N over V m v bar squared
half m v bar squared equals three halves k B T

steps.memory_tip: ⅓ becomes ⅔ of a HALF: PV = ⅓Nmv̄² = ⅔N(½mv̄²).

steps.label: Kinetic interpretation of temperature
lines: The ideal gas equation for N molecules
is PV = N k_B T. Comparing the two
expressions for PV,

lines.text: ⅔ N (½ m v̄²) = N k_B T

lines: The absolute temperature is a direct
measure of the average translational
kinetic energy of a molecule — nothing
else.
steps.margin_note: Eighth mark. State the meaning in words too — temperature measures average kinetic energy, not pressure or volume.
steps.why: This is the payoff of the whole derivation: kinetic theory and the gas equation both describe the same gas, so setting their two expressions for PV equal reveals what temperature actually IS at the molecular level.
common_mistakes: Leaving out the ½ and writing mv̄² = (3/2)k_BT — the ½ is part of the kinetic energy on the left.
Saying temperature depends on the gas or its pressure — the result shows it depends on neither.

recall.must_convey: That comparing PV = two thirds N half m v bar squared with PV = N k B T gives half m v bar squared equals three halves k B T, so absolute temperature measures the average translational kinetic energy of a molecule.
accept: half m v bar squared equals three halves k B T
comparing with PV equals N k B T
temperature measures the average kinetic energy
the N cancels leaving half m v bar squared
this is the kinetic interpretation of temperature
reject: P equals one third N over V m v bar squared
force is m v x squared over L

steps.memory_tip: Equate the two PV expressions, cancel N, then divide by ⅔ — dividing by two-thirds is what turns k_BT into (3/2)k_BT.

insider_note: Every one of the eight steps earns its own mark, so do not skip the isotropy argument or the ½ inside the energy rewrite — both are where marks are usually lost.
